Stakeholder / outside-view note · Maps to Course 04 (Competitive Strategy: coopetition with alternatives managers, market makers and venues who are clients, partners and rivals at once), Course 08 (Negotiation: reading the other side's incentives in a testimonial or a podcast answer), E8 (Stakeholder & Investor Relations: whose voice gets printed on the firm's own channels, and why) · Written 2026-10-25 · Part of goldman hub; companions goldman people, goldman mission forces, goldman awm private credit, goldman digital assets; Tradeweb counterpart tradeweb outside voices

  • Source: _ingest/raw/goldman/articles.jsonl (262 items, Jan 2019 – Oct 2026), searched for every non-GS speaker, then checked against the reader notes A–G. By my count about 17 hosted items carry external guests: Top of Mind issues and their podcasts (crypto May 2021, crypto winter Dec 2022, gen-AI Jun 2024, stablecoins Aug–Sep 2025, private credit Apr–May 2026) and Exchanges / Great Investors episodes (Rowan 2023, Arougheti 2024, Aronson 2025, Craver, Zelter and Griffin 2026). About 15 press releases carry partner or counterparty quotes (CCP paper ×2, AWS, AmEx, Datonomy, Visual Structuring, GS DAP, BNY, GreenSky sale, T. Rowe Price, QIA, plus the AWM targets). Gaps: the Dec-2022 Top of Mind is a redacted scrape, so Clayton, Massad, Kasumovich and Gorton survive only as cover pull-quotes. There is no earnings-call Q&A, so no sell-side analyst ever speaks. No 10-K or press coverage was used.
  • Selection-bias warning (it applies to every line below): every voice here sits on a Goldman-owned channel with a Goldman host: Allison Nathan (Research), Jake Siewert (Communications), Alison Mass (chairman of Investment Banking), Tony Pasquariello, Raj Mahajan, George Lee, Michael Brandmeyer. Guests are chosen, edited and published by the firm, and transcripts carry the disclaimer that views are the interviewee's own. The skeptics are invited: most argue about a theme (AI capex, crypto, stablecoins, private credit), almost never about Goldman. Partner quotes are co-written releases. Read every line as what this speaker was willing to say on Goldman's microphone. The few lines that do cut against the house view count for more because they got through.
  • Core claim: The outside voices fall into three bands. (1) Invited skeptics (Acemoglu, Roubini, Eichengreen, Gorton, plus in-house Covello) let Goldman own both sides of every theme it also earns fees from. Their objections are real and, read in order, they pre-critique Goldman's later moves: Roubini's blockchain in name only (2021) before GS DAP's "permissioned distributed technologies" (2024); Gorton's interoperability warning (2022) before the BNY tokenized-MMF bridge (2025); Covello's "$1tn problem" (2024) before OneGS 3.0 (2025). (2) Alternatives managers and market makers (Marks, Arougheti, Zelter, Rowan, Aronson, Griffin, Craver) are clients, borrowers' financiers and competitors at once. They talk their own book, and the sharpest strategic line in the corpus is Rowan's: the "new banks" are investors. (3) Partners and co-signers (Apple by silence, BNY, Tradeweb, AWS, MSCI, AmEx, Sixth Street, T. Rowe, QIA; BlackRock, JPM, Vanguard, Guardian on CCPs) praise the rail or the deal, never Goldman as indispensable. My reading of the power map (inference): the Federal Reserve (sets the stress capital buffer that sets the dividend) and the large asset managers and alternatives giants hold the most leverage. Then come Citadel Securities–type market makers and the rail partners Goldman needed to mutualize GS DAP. Goldman holds power mainly over the founders it buys (Industry Ventures, Innovator, NEOS, LCN) and the managers it launches. Absent: regulators in their own voice, unhappy clients, Marcus customers, rival dealers and venues.

1. Stakeholder map

Quotes verbatim, ≤25 words, dated by corpus date unless noted. Letters are dated to fiscal year-end but published ~Mar–Apr of the next year. "Incentive read" is my inference throughout.

Group Named voices What they want from Goldman What they said (dated) Incentive read

2. The invited skeptics — what they argued, and what Goldman did next

Read in date order, the skeptics form a running critique of Goldman's own strategy, published on Goldman's own channels before the firm acted.

Skeptic (date) Argument (verbatim where quoted) What Goldman did afterwards Read (inference)
Roubini (May 24 2021) Enterprise ledgers are blockchain in name only. "Any treasurer who invests in something that falls 15% in value overnight will be fired." Nov 18 2024: plans to spin GS DAP out as industry-owned; McDermott: "We view permissioned distributed technologies as the next structural change to financial markets" GS chose exactly the permissioned model Roubini dismissed, then gave up ownership. That concedes half his point: a single-firm ledger is not trusted
Alan Cohen (May 24 2021) Anonymity will meet regulatory opposition GS's crypto access stayed cash-settled and regulated (CME futures, NDFs); DAP is permissioned Consistent with Cohen; GS treated regulated status as a moat
Gorton (Dec 13 2022) Contagion was contained only by disconnection: "But that lack of interoperability will eventually change." Jul 23 2025: BNY × GS tokenized MMFs, mirror tokens on GS DAP; McDermott wants to "unlock their utility as a form of collateral" GS is building the bridge Gorton said would carry the next contagion. Nobody on the channel connects the two
Clayton / Massad (Dec 13 2022) Unregulated markets are dangerous; state regimes are pre-1929 GS waited: no GS strategy statement on crypto from 2023 to mid-2024 in the corpus Silence during the Gensler-era SEC is itself a stance
Acemoglu (Jun 25 2024) AI touches ~4.6% of tasks in a decade; new-task creation is "not a law of nature" 2025 OneGS 3.0, our new operating model propelled by AI (2025 letter); then Solomon: "the reality of it is that it's narrower than that grand vision of reimagining the firm." (Jan 23 2026) Goldman adopted the bull's language and the skeptic's expectations
Covello (Jun 25 2024) AI is expensive by design; "revisionist history" to assume it gets cheap; stay long chips because bubbles last About $500bn of AI-related debt was issued in 2026 YTD, ~18% of IG supply (GS Research credit podcast, Aug 5 2026): a fee pool for GBM's underwriters and credit desk The skeptic's call was on returns to adopters; the firm earns on the spend either way (inference)
Eichengreen (Sep 2 2025) "So, what's at risk is what economists refer to as a singleness of money." GS's cash leg is a tokenized MMF with BNY as official record-keeper, not a GS stablecoin Goldman's design choice sits on Eichengreen's side of the argument; Brooks's side won the legislation (GENIUS Act)
Marks (May 11 2026) "Liquidity is a problem whenever a vehicle that invests in private assets promises liquidity." GS kept buying private-markets and wrapper businesses through the stress: LCN (Aug 18 2026), NEOS (Aug 12 2026 dateline), T. Rowe target-date funds due mid-2026 GS's own answer agrees with Marks on the product: Bantwal: "But the reality is that it's not semiliquid, it's illiquid." (Mar 23 2026)

Inside voices that concede an outside point (scarce, therefore weighted up): - Solomon on the 2020 plan: "We haven't executed perfectly on all of them. And there are places where we certainly could have executed better." (Feb 24 2023). The only critics he names in seven letters are the unnamed ones who made "calls to downsize our Global Markets business" (2020 letter). - Solomon on private credit and AI-exposed software: "are a reminder that the credit cycle has not been repealed." (2025 letter). That is Marks's point, a year earlier, in the CEO's voice. - Bantwal: "There are a lot of new players in private credit that haven’t been tested through cycles." (Mar 26 2026). - Varadhan on where risk moved: "so much of our workflow has migrated through technological automation" (Nov 21 2023). - Churchman on AI and the junior pipeline: "there's a huge danger here that in the era of AI, we outsource our reasoning to these models, and we have cognitive atrophy" (Aug 24 2026). - Osman Ali, against the AI-efficiency consensus: "these models, again, in the hands of the average person will create herd behavior" (May 6 2026).

Pattern: the skeptics win the expectations argument and lose the allocation argument. Goldman lowers its rhetoric (Solomon's "narrower", Bantwal's "illiquid") while it keeps spending, buying and financing. That is consistent with a firm that earns fees on both sides of every theme.

3. Alternatives managers and market makers — clients, competitors, the "new banks"

What they agree on. Every alternatives guest in 2026 argues the stress is technical, not fundamental. Zelter: "I think the market is missing what it really is." (Apr 16 2026). Arougheti: "So there is no asset liability mismatch, there is no run on the bank in these funds." (Apr 29 2026). Marks, the nearest to a skeptic, still calls the software hit bad rather than systemic. Goldman's own voices say the same. Lynam on 5%-a-quarter redemption limits: "they are a feature, not a bug" (Apr 29 2026). There is no internal or external dissent on whether private credit is systemic. That should make a reader more cautious, not less.

What they reveal about the dealer's position. - Rowan (Feb 10 2023) gives the dealer's core strategic problem in two lines: "we have roughly the same amount of dealer capital, our market making capital today as we did in 2008." Markets, he says, are three times bigger. And: "So, who are the new banks? Investors." From a dealer's seat this is a threat and a business. Capital Solutions Group (Jan 2025) is Goldman's attempt to originate for the new banks rather than compete with them (goldman awm private credit). - Arougheti (Jul 23 2024): "we say no to our clients 95 percent of the time." Origination discipline is the edge. Zelter makes the same point about origination as the bottleneck. Both are describing the scarce input that Goldman's banking franchise supplies. - Aronson (Sep 3 2025): "But I always leave the last nickel on the table. Always." A seller's maxim on Goldman's Great Investors show, from a manager whose structured-equity product competes with bank financing. - Griffin (Jul 9 2026) is the only voice from a non-bank rival to Goldman's markets business. He says compute is now a core input to market making: "people who have lower margin businesses won't be able to bear that cost impact". That is a scale argument that cuts toward Citadel Securities and the largest dealers alike. He also ribs the host firm on its own podcast. - Craver (Feb 12 2026): "I used to be able to read a press release and tell you what the stock was going to do the next day." Passive and multi-strategy flow have hollowed out fundamental price discovery. For Goldman this is a tailwind: it finances the multi-strats and makes markets in the ETFs (wss trading hedge funds).

Incentive read (inference): each of these guests is simultaneously a client of GBM (financing, prime, coverage), a counterparty to GSAM (co-investor, competitor for LP dollars) and, for Griffin, a direct rival for market-making share. None has an incentive to criticise Goldman on air, and none does.

Issue Bulls Skeptics / regulators Goldman's own line

Novogratz (crypto is an official asset class; Uniswap vs CME); Sonnenshein (only plumbing is missing) Roubini; Cohen; Dan Guido: "It’s a wild west out there for developers building applications on the blockchain." Aug–Sep 2025, stablecoins Brooks: "Well, it depends on if you trust your betters or if you'd rather be free." Eichengreen: singleness of money; no deposit insurance McDermott: "the narrative has been that “the institutions are coming.”" (Jun 10 2025)

Read: the guests track the cycle. Bulls dominate the 2021 peak, ex-regulators the 2022 crash, and a pro-stablecoin ex-regulator debates an academic in the 2025 legislative window. Goldman's own line moves underneath, from access (2021) to plumbing (2022–25), and never needs to say a guest was right or wrong. The FTX moment is the one time the corpus lets regulators frame the issue, and those pages are the ones that survive only as cover quotes.

How the hosts frame the guests over time:

Period Dominant frame on GS channels Representative host or guest line

6. The CCP co-signers — the clearest dealers-and-users vs infrastructure stance

The Oct 24 2019 paper was signed by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, Allianz, Citi, Societe Generale, State Street, T. Rowe Price and Vanguard. Ten more joined on Mar 10 2020 (ABN AMRO Clearing, Barclays, Deutsche Bank, CBA, Franklin Templeton, Guardian Life, Ivy, Nordea, TIAA, UBS). It asks CCPs to put their own capital into the default waterfall in two tranches and caps assessments at one times a member's default-fund contribution. Goldman's Nicolas Friedman frames it as "aligning incentives and enhancing financial stability through even stronger CCPs". BlackRock's Kiely wants CCPs "optimally structured". Vanguard's Thum asks for "additional protections to strengthen margin calculations and default fund components".

Read (inference): this is the one place where buy-side and sell-side speak with one voice, and the target is market infrastructure owned by exchange groups (the CCP owners are never named). No CCP is quoted. For a dealer, CCP rules are a cost line and a tail risk. Pushing loss-absorption onto the CCP's own capital moves risk from members to exchange shareholders. Compare Tradeweb's position on Treasury clearing (tradeweb derivatives regulation): the venue warns about margin stress, while the dealers here want the CCP to carry more of it.

7. The institutional counterweights — heard only through Goldman

  • Federal Reserve. It appears as the source of a number, never as a speaker. The 2020 SCB of 6.7% was revised to 6.6% after a Fed calculation error (Sep 4 2020). Solomon publicly disputed the 2024 figure: "This increase does not seem to reflect the strategic evolution of our business" (Jun 28 2024). Then, after the SCB fell to 3.4%, he praised the Fed's intent "to institute a more transparent and fair approach to these tests" (Jul 1 2025). The Fed's own reasoning is absent.
  • DOJ and US/UK/Singapore/Hong Kong regulators (1MDB). Heard through Solomon's memo ("we recognize that we did not adequately address red flags", Oct 22 2020) and the Board: "The Board views the 1MDB matter as an institutional failure, inconsistent with the high expectations it has for the Firm."
  • Government of Malaysia. Heard through the settlement terms: $2.5bn paid plus a guarantee of at least $1.4bn in asset recoveries, and "the Government of Malaysia agreed to withdraw the pending criminal charges" (Jul 24 2020).

Read: these are the only actors who imposed costs on Goldman without its consent: $3.42bn of 2020 litigation provisions, about $174m of compensation clawbacks and cuts, a capital buffer that moved 330bp from its first print (derived: 6.7% → 3.4%; the 2025 letter says 320bp, measuring from the revised 6.6%). They are also the only ones with no microphone. That is the clearest measure of what the channel is for.

8. Power map (inference)

Dependence = importance × lack of alternatives (canon pfeffer power).

Actor What Goldman needs from them Alternatives Goldman has Leverage over GS
Federal Reserve Capital headroom: SCB sets the CET1 floor, and the floor sets buybacks and the dividend ($0.85 in 2019 → $5.00 in 2026) None Highest
Large asset managers (BlackRock, Vanguard, T. Rowe) Flow, mandates, co-signers on market-structure fights, a 401(k) channel Few at this scale High. They sit on both sides: clients and allies on CCPs, competitors in asset management
Alternatives giants (Apollo, Ares, Oaktree, Sixth Street) Sponsor and financing fees; buyers for assets GS exits (GreenSky) Some, but the sponsor wallet is concentrated High and rising: they are the "new banks"
Non-bank market makers (Citadel Securities) Nothing directly; they compete for the same flow and are also prime clients — Medium. Griffin's compute argument says only the scaled survive, which includes GS
Rail partners (Tradeweb, BNY, Digital Asset) Neutrality and adoption for GS DAP Few: a GS-only rail failed the adoption test Medium, on the digital-asset bet only
Big Tech (Apple, AWS) Distribution (Apple), cloud and talent (AWS) Apple: none once it left. AWS: other clouds Medium–high in consumer (now exited); medium in tech
Sovereign anchors (QIA) $25bn of capital Other sovereigns Medium; priced in Doha headcount
Acquired founders (Industry Ventures, Innovator, NEOS, LCN) Product and wrappers Build instead of buy Low: earn-outs and GS stock tie them in

Read: Goldman's leverage is greatest where it is buyer or host and weakest where it needs permission (Fed), distribution (Apple, T. Rowe, BNY) or neutrality (Tradeweb). The consumer exit is a case of that map: every party it depended on had alternatives, and Goldman had none.

9. What is conspicuously absent

  • Regulators in their own voice. No sitting Fed, SEC, CFTC, OCC, PRA or FCA official speaks. The ex-officials (Clayton, Massad, Brooks, Cohen) speak as private citizens, and Cohen is a former GS compliance head. Gensler appears only paraphrased.
  • Unhappy clients. No client says it moved business away, paid too much or was badly served. The anonymous client quotes in the Investor Day 2023 deck are testimonials.
  • Marcus customers. "Marcus" appears in 21 items, always in management's voice. No depositor, borrower or Apple Card holder speaks. The customer-assistance program of 2020 is described, not heard.
  • Rival dealers. JPMorgan appears as a CCP co-signer and as the buyer of the Apple Card book, never as a competitor. Morgan Stanley appears twice, in a peer table and a résumé.
  • Venues. MarketAxess, ICE, Trumid and Jane Street are never named. Tradeweb appears in two items. CME appears only as the venue for crypto futures. The ICE–MarketAxess deal (Jul 30 2026) and Tradeweb–Trumid (Oct 19 2026, on which Goldman advised Trumid per tradeweb strategy financials) do not exist on Goldman's channels.
  • The CCPs, whom the 2019 paper targets.
  • Short-sellers, sell-side analysts and the press. The press appears only as something to rebut (Varadhan on departures, 2020; Bantwal on private-credit coverage not "necessarily nuanced or accurate", Mar 26 2026).
  • Employees below partner, ex-partners and 1MDB counterparties.

10. Canon lenses

  • Power and dependence (canon pfeffer power): §8. Goldman's leverage is as buyer and host. The Fed, Apple and the big asset managers each score high on importance and on Goldman's lack of alternatives.
  • Coopetition (canon brandenburger nalebuff coopetition): Apollo, Ares and Citadel are clients, competitors and complementors at once. BlackRock is a client, an asset-management rival and a CCP co-signer. Tradeweb is a DAP partner, a co-investor in Digital Asset and the venue Goldman quotes on.
  • Testimonials and authority (canon cialdini influence): the partner quotes are social proof for the category. Discount the acquired founders' quotes (Innovator, LCN) the way you discount a reference from a relative.
  • Agency (canon jensen meckling agency theory): alternatives guests are agents for their LPs and their own fee streams. "Not systemic" is the line every one of them needs.
  • Selection and WYSIATI (canon kahneman thinking fast and slow): a curated sample. The absence of regulators, clients and rivals is not evidence that they agree.
  • Lemons and disclosure (canon akerlof market for lemons): Marks's question about whether retail buyers were adequately informed is a lemons problem in a semi-liquid wrapper.

Role-play: you sit on T. Rowe Price's retirement investment committee. The co-branded target-date funds with a Goldman private-markets sleeve are due to launch (mid-2026, per the Sep 4 2025 release). Private credit is in its 2026 stress. Using only the voices above, put five questions to Goldman's private-credit co-heads, one line each: 1. Liquidity promise: 'Your own co-head says the asset is "not semiliquid, it's illiquid". What liquidity does the sleeve promise a 401(k) participant, and who funds it on a bad day?' 2. Allocation conflict: 'Capital Solutions originates and GSAM invests. Which loans go to your funds and which to third-party clients, and who decides?' 3. Software exposure: 'Marks and Bantwal both put software at roughly a quarter of direct lending. Show the sleeve's share and the loan-to-value at today's marks, not origination.' 4. Marks and alpha: 'Brandmeyer says PE alpha has gone negative. Why should the private-credit marks be faster to fall than the PE marks were?' 5. Disclosure: 'Marks asks whether buyers were adequately informed. What will our participants be told about redemption limits that Arougheti says are "not really a gate"?'

Then compute (worked answers): - Marks's arithmetic. A fund with 25% in software loses half the value of that slice. Loss = 0.25 × 0.5 = 12.5% of assets. Levered 1:1 (assets = 2 × equity), the equity loss = 25%. - Arougheti's absorption test. Maximum non-traded BDC redemptions ≈ $5bn a quarter of loan sales against ≈ $85bn a quarter of syndicated-loan trading: 5 / 85 = 5.9% of quarterly secondary volume (derived). A 5%-a-quarter cap compounds to at most 1 − 0.95⁴ = 18.5% of NAV a year if every quarter fills, a little under the nominal 20% (derived). - Blostein's gap (Mar 23 2026). $50–70bn of expected outflow against $40–45bn of liquid holdings in retail vehicles leaves a shortfall of $5bn to $30bn that must come from loan sales, new inflows or deferral (derived).

Decide: launch on schedule, delay a year, or launch with a smaller private sleeve. Then name which voice in this note you would weight most, and why its incentive makes it more or less credible (canon pfeffer power).
